title: Marmalade's Midnight Adventure
markdown:
Every night, when Lily’s breathing slowed to the small tide of sleep, the room changed its mind about what it was for. Toys found their joints. Pets found the floor. Plans that had been only whisker-twitches in daylight stood up and asked to be walked.

Marmalade the bunny was staring at the cookie jar. It sat on the kitchen counter like a moon someone had forgotten to hang, glass catching the night-light in a ring that looked almost reachable. His tail gave one hopeful twitch. He wriggled his nose, then his whiskers, as if scent alone might lower the lid. The smell was butter and sugar and the particular promise of a thing kept too high. He crouched until his hind legs trembled, sprang, and met only smooth ceramic. His paws scrabbled. He slid down in a heap of fluff and landed with a bounce that would have been comic if he had not wanted the cookie so badly. He sat very still on the tiles, feeling wobbly and determined in the same breath. Jumping, he decided, was not the only tool a bunny owned.

Lily snored the soft unused snore of someone who had drawn all afternoon. Marmalade hopped to Walnut, the teddy with one slightly loose button eye, and to Aurelia, whose moonlight-white coat caught the night-light and tried to improve it. “The stars are out,” Marmalade said, nose working the cooler air from the hall. “And she left her map.” He nudged a crumpled drawing across the rug: a river like a blue scribble, a patch of woods that had used up the green crayon, and a circle labelled Midnight Picnic in letters that leaned as if they were already walking.

“An adventure,” Marmalade said, as if the word itself were a biscuit.

Walnut sighed, a rustle of stuffing. “It is rather late. And woods can be… woody.”

Aurelia tossed her mane, a cascade that made the night-light look modest. “Naturally we shall go. I shall keep the proceedings polite, and I shall keep a careful eye.”

They eased the front door just wide enough for fluff, felt, and a horn. Dew cooled their paws. The garden smelled of cut grass and the last of the day, a green sweetness that had nowhere left to go. Beyond the fence the old woods waited along the river path, a place of rustle and pocket-dark, ordinary by noon and enormous now. Sleeping birds made no comment. A moth tested the porch light and thought better of it.

Trees closed over them like a leafy argument that had been settled long ago. Moonlight broke on the path in coins. The earth smelled damp and used. Marmalade, busy with the leaf-whisper and the idea of a picnic that existed because a child had drawn it, nearly hooked a gnarled root with his foot. He yelped; his tail performed a startled zigzag. A violin answered from a mossy log: sad, then skipping, then sad again, as if it could not decide which evening it belonged to. A fox sat there with the instrument tucked under his chin, whiskers keeping time, the bow moving as if the night had hired him. The tune was good enough to startle. Marmalade stumbled. The map left his paws and spun toward a patch of dark soil that would have eaten the crayon river without noticing.

“Oh no.”

Walnut’s paw stopped it a breath before the dirt. “Steady.”

The fox flourished his bow, pleased to have provided a soundtrack, and played on, a little louder, as if applause might yet arrive.

They came to a fork where the moonlight seemed to split its mind. One way went into deeper shadow, twisty, the sort of path that looked like a mistake until you were on it. The other glittered as if someone had spilled a jar of light and called it guidance. Aurelia pointed a delicate hoof at the bright one. “Superior light. Simply logical. One can always rely on it.”

Marmalade’s tummy wobbled with the same not-sure feeling he had met under the cookie jar. He remembered how Lily’s river had curved on the paper, a loop that did not match the glitter. “I think it is this way,” he said, and nodded at the darker path, a hunch tickling his whiskers. Aurelia’s snort was tiny and amused. “Your perception is charmingly limited.” They followed her light anyway, because a unicorn announcing a path has a kind of weather to it. After a few minutes the path ended in brambles, sharp and uninterested in logic. Thorns held a few of Aurelia’s sparkles as trophies.

Marmalade looked back. The bright way had been a performance. He thought of the jar and the bounce and the decision not to keep jumping at the same height. He took a breath of damp air. “The other way,” he said, smaller, then firmer. He tilted the map as if it might whisper. “This feels right.”

It did. The darker path unspooled, root by root, to the familiar bend of the riverbank: wet stones, a smell of weed and cool, the water making the small talk it always made. Walnut’s button eye warmed. Aurelia said nothing about superior light.

The woods thickened after that. Branches made fingers. Twigs snapped where no one was walking. Something watched without introducing itself. Aurelia, still smarting from the brambles, pranced harder, hooves barely touching, as if radiance could undo a wrong turn. Sparkles shook from her mane like a private firework. Eyes opened in the ferns: one pair, then three, ember-small, curious in a way that was not quite friendly. Walnut said, quietly, “We need not be the brightest things tonight.” Aurelia’s coat took on the faint colour of embarrassment. She stopped showing off. They hurried. Marmalade wanted, for a moment, a burrow of moss and no observers, the cookie jar’s failure suddenly a simpler problem than being looked at.

The clearing arrived all the same. Lily’s circle, translated into real grass. No blanket. No waiting friends. No feast laid out by anyone who had read the drawing. Dew, moon, and one old oak that had been practising stillness for longer than picnics. Marmalade’s ears lowered. “Empty.”

Walnut sat down beside him, a useful weight. “We are here. And we packed.”

Aurelia did not lecture the clearing on dashed expectations. Her horn made a modest lamp of the dewdrops. She looked at the oak, then at the two of them, and her voice came down a notch. “The drawing got us walking.”

They spread Lily’s crumbly cheese biscuits and two plump carrots on a flat stone that had been waiting for a purpose. The fox, who had followed at a polite distance, stepped to the edge of the trees and played something slower, a tune that fitted an empty place better than a fanfare. No flourish this time. Marmalade ate. The cheese smell was ordinary and perfect, a kitchen fact in a wood. On the path they would take later, Aurelia’s horn-light would catch in wet leaves and look, for a few steps, like a dropped string of stars. He did not announce what that meant. He passed Walnut a biscuit that was mostly crumbs. Aurelia, for once, did not improve the arrangement or rename the picnic. The oak kept its secrets. The fox found a last quiet phrase and let it end. They packed the empty napkin, such as it was, and turned toward home with crumbs on their fur and the map, rescued twice, folded small enough to believe in again.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
